content:
Gunmen opened fire on tourists in a meadow near the resort town of Pahalgam in Indian-administered Kashmir, killing 26 people and wounding at least 17, police said, in the worst attack on civilians in the disputed region in nearly two decades. The dead included 25 Indians and one Nepalese national, according to police, and the shooting took place in the Baisaran Valley, a meadow about 90 kilometres from Srinagar that is popular with visitors on horseback. Witnesses told AFP the gunmen emerged from a forest near the meadow and fired on the tourists, sparing women and shooting men, while dozens fled in panic and local guides carried the wounded away on ponies.

A previously little-known militant group calling itself the Kashmir Resistance claimed responsibility for the attack in a message on social media, and later said those targeted were not ordinary tourists but people linked to Indian security agencies. Indian security agencies say the group is a front for Pakistan-based militant organisations such as Lashkar-e-Taiba and Hizbul Mujahideen, although no evidence has been publicly produced. Prime Minister Narendra Modi condemned what he called a "heinous act" and pledged that the attackers "will be brought to justice", while Home Minister Amit Shah flew to Kashmir and vowed the harshest consequences for those responsible. Jammu and Kashmir Chief Minister Omar Abdullah called the attack "an abomination" and said it was "much larger than anything we've seen directed at civilians in recent years".

India moved within a day, announcing a sweeping downgrade of its relationship with Pakistan. Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri told reporters that the Cabinet Committee on Security, chaired by Modi, had found that the attack had "cross-border" links to Pakistan, and set out a series of measures: the 1960 Indus Waters Treaty would be held in abeyance "until Pakistan credibly and irrevocably abjures its support for cross-border terrorism"; the only functioning land border crossing, the Integrated Check Post at Attari, would be closed; all visas issued to Pakistani nationals would be revoked; Pakistani defence advisers in New Delhi were declared persona non grata and given a week to leave; and staffing at both countries' missions would be cut from 55 to 30. The attack came during a four-day visit to India by US Vice President JD Vance, who called it a "devastating terrorist attack" and offered condolences to the victims.

Pakistan denied any connection to the attack and answered with countermeasures of its own. Islamabad called India's blame "frivolous [and] devoid of rationality", closed its airspace to all Indian-owned or Indian-operated airlines, suspended all trade with India including trade routed through third countries, and cancelled visas issued to Indian nationals. Pakistan also warned it could suspend its participation in all bilateral agreements with India, including the 1972 Simla Agreement that has underpinned relations between the two countries since the war that led to the creation of Bangladesh. Islamabad has since called for a neutral investigation into the attack, pledging to cooperate with any impartial inquiry.

The confrontation has already spilled onto the ground. Indian officials said troops exchanged fire with Pakistani soldiers along the highly militarised frontier in Kashmir late on Thursday, after Pakistani soldiers fired at an Indian position and Indian soldiers retaliated; no casualties were reported. Indian forces have fanned out across the region in a manhunt for the attackers, and residents and police in southern Kashmir said soldiers demolished the family homes of two suspected militants accused of involvement in the attack. Tourists have been leaving the valley in large numbers, with airlines operating extra flights from Srinagar, and the Indian army said its search operation was continuing with all efforts focused on bringing the perpetrators to justice.

At the centre of the crisis sits the Indus Waters Treaty, the World Bank-brokered agreement from 1960 that divides the waters of the Indus river system between the two countries and has survived two wars and decades of hostility. For Pakistan, whose agriculture depends heavily on those rivers, any sustained interruption would be a grave threat, and Islamabad has warned that disrupting its water supply would be considered an act of war. Legal experts, however, question whether India can do what it has announced: as [Al Jazeera reported](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2025/4/24/kashmir-attack-does-indias-indus-waters-treaty-freeze-threaten-pakistan), the treaty contains no provision for holding it "in abeyance", and it can only be modified by mutual agreement between the two parties. The treaty has no designated enforcement body, which leaves the standoff in untested legal territory.

The attack is a setback for the picture of returning calm that Modi's government has promoted since revoking Jammu and Kashmir's limited autonomy in 2019, after which the authorities heavily promoted the mountainous region as a holiday destination. Around 3.5 million tourists visited Kashmir in 2024, according to official figures, and India hosted a G20 tourism meeting in Srinagar in 2023 in a bid to show that normalcy had returned. India keeps an estimated 500,000 soldiers permanently deployed in the territory, but fighting had decreased in recent years, and attacks deliberately targeting tourists have been rare. The deadliest recent attack on civilians before this one was in March 2000, when 36 people were killed, while the worst attack in recent years overall was at Pulwama in February 2019, when 40 paramilitary police were killed in a car bombing.

What happens next will turn on whether either side steps back from measures that are easy to announce and hard to reverse. Pakistan's call for a neutral probe offers one off-ramp, but neither government has shown signs of softening, and the exchange of fire along the Line of Control shows how quickly a diplomatic crisis can become a military one between two nuclear-armed neighbours that have fought three wars over Kashmir. The episode also lands at a sensitive moment for New Delhi's wider diplomacy, with a major trade agreement with Washington delayed, as covered in our report on the [India-US trade deal](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/india-us-trade-deal-signing-delayed-november-2026), and with India's military modernisation under scrutiny, including the [Rafale fleet assessment](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/india-rafale-active-fleet-cut-32-flightglobal-november-2026). For now, the border is closed, the water treaty is in limbo, the airspace is shut, and the families of 26 people are mourning a holiday that ended in a meadow in Pahalgam.
summary: Gunmen killed 26 tourists near Pahalgam in Indian-administered Kashmir, the worst attack on civilians there in nearly two decades. India blamed Pakistan, suspended the 1960 Indus Waters Treaty, closed the only land border crossing and revoked Pakistani visas; Pakistan denied involvement, closed its airspace, suspended trade and called for a neutral probe, as troops exchanged fire along the Line of Control.
title: India and Pakistan slide toward confrontation after Kashmir attack kills 26 tourists
